Neonates of the Winter skate (Leucoraja ocellata) emerge from their egg cases with a disc width of approximately 17 cm [Lb = approximately 17 cm], a dimension that reflects the considerable yolk reserves these young elasmobranchs depend upon before commencing independent foraging. This size at birth is relatively large when compared to many other skate species of similar adult dimensions, suggesting a strategy of investing substantial maternal resources into each individual offspring. Following the absorption of their yolk sacs, these pups must successfully locate and capture benthic invertebrates to sustain themselves, a critical transition that occurs during their first weeks of life. Field studies conducted in the northwestern Atlantic have shown that these neonates are born in shallow, coastal nursery grounds, where food availability is typically high and predation pressure from larger piscivores may be somewhat reduced. Understanding the precise disc width at parturition is essential for fisheries managers who aim to protect these critical early life stages from trawling activities, as individuals of this size are particularly vulnerable to capture in bottom nets.

At the stable temperatures that characterize their deep-water habitat (7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]), the gestation period for Winter skate lasts approximately 620 days [ab = approximately 620 days], an exceptionally prolonged developmental phase for an elasmobranch. This lengthy incubation is consistent with the species' cold-water environment and its slow, energy-conserving life history strategy. During this extended period, the developing embryo relies entirely upon the nutrients contained within the large, protein-rich yolk sac, growing steadily until it reaches a size capable of independent survival upon hatching. The protracted age at birth contrasts sharply with the shorter gestation periods reported for many temperate and tropical sharks, highlighting how thermal regimes can profoundly influence reproductive phenology. For populations inhabiting the colder, deeper portions of the skate's range, this duration may be further extended, as metabolic rates and hence developmental velocities are closely tied to ambient water temperature. The exact timing of parturition, however, also depends on the size and condition of the gravid female at the time of egg deposition.

Female Winter skate attain sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 74.5 cm [Lp = approximately 74.5 cm], a size that corresponds to roughly two-thirds of the species' ultimate total length. This threshold, which can range between 73 and 76 cm depending on local environmental conditions and food availability, marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the first production of viable oocytes. The length at puberty is a critical parameter for population models, as it determines the proportion of the stock that is reproductively active at any given time. In heavily exploited regions, where larger, older individuals are selectively removed by fishing gear, the average size at maturity has been observed to shift subtly, potentially as a density-dependent response to reduced competition for resources. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from specimens collected across the species' range confirms that females below this length rarely exhibit signs of follicular development, emphasizing the importance of protecting individuals above this size threshold to ensure continued recruitment. The corresponding length at which males mature is slightly smaller, though the precise values are less well-documented in the published literature.

The maximum reprod rate for this species, derived from fecundity and frequency data, indicates that females produce approximately one clutch every 28 days [F_R_i = approximately one clutch every 28 days] during the peak of the reproductive season, with each clutch containing a single egg case [N_R_i = a single egg case]. This reproductive output, parameterized at a water temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], is among the lowest recorded for any marine elasmobranch, reflecting a life history strategy centered on the production of very few, well-provisioned offspring. The rate is modeled on a kap value of 0.7, a theoretical constant that describes the fraction of available resources allocated to somatic growth versus reproduction in standard bioenergetic frameworks. Given the long gestation period and the extended time required for females to replenish their energy stores between reproductive events, the realized annual fecundity is quite modest. This slow reproductive turnover makes the Winter skate particularly vulnerable to overfishing, as populations cannot quickly recover from even modest increases in adult mortality. Tagging studies have confirmed that mature females may skip breeding seasons entirely in years when prey is scarce.

The maximum lifespan of Winter skate in the wild is estimated at approximately 21 years [am = approximately 21 years] when measured at an environmental temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C], a longevity that is typical for slow-growing, late-maturing elasmobranchs inhabiting cold-temperate waters. This extended lifespan, combined with a late age at first reproduction and low fecundity, places the species firmly within the category of K-selected organisms whose populations are highly sensitive to perturbations in adult survival rates. Archived data from vertebral band counts, validated through bomb radiocarbon dating, have confirmed ages exceeding two decades for some of the largest individuals captured in research trawls. The ultimate total length reached by this species is approximately 110 cm [Li = approximately 110 cm], a size that is rarely attained in heavily fished regions where mortality truncates the older age classes. Preserved specimens from early twentieth-century surveys, before intensive commercial exploitation, suggest that historical maximum lengths may have been slightly greater, indicating a potential shift in population demographics. Protecting the oldest, largest individuals is therefore a conservation priority, as these animals contribute disproportionately to the reproductive output of the population.
